title: loop.sh treats a wrapper exit as proof the agent is gone, and orphans its process group
body:
## What happened

At 2026-09-07T00:15Z a dev-loop worker was stopped. `loop.sh` reported, correctly as far as it
could see:

    Terminated
    Agent exited nonzero (status 143) — failing this cycle.
    ✗ cycle 2 made no committed progress (2/5 consecutive, 2/15 total).
    Graceful stop requested (ai-runs/loop.stop) — cycle 2 is finished and pushed; exiting.

The loop then exited. **The agent did not.** The `claude` child (pid 27275, PGID 27260) ignored
SIGTERM, was reparented to init, and kept running with `--permission-mode acceptEdits` in the
PRIMARY checkout for **18 minutes 48 seconds** after the driver had declared the cycle failed and
gone away. It wrote two tracked source files while nothing was supervising it:

    src/world/local_job_scene.ts    00:30:17.951
    src/world/session_local_view.ts 00:30:38.767

A `SIGKILL` to the pid plus `pkill -9 -P` cleared it; the checkout was reverted with
`git checkout --` and the stray work preserved outside the repo.

## Why this is a driver defect, not an operator mistake

`loop.sh` waits on the agent command (`dev-agent.sh`), not on its process group. A wrapper's exit
status is therefore **not** evidence that the agent is gone — the wrapper can exit 143 while its
grandchild runs on. That inference is baked into the driver in two places:

1. the hang-kill path (`AI_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default 2400), which is the automatic case and
   fires with no human watching;
2. the graceful-stop path, which then exits the loop entirely, releasing the single-writer guard
   in `ai-runs/loop.pid` while a writer is still alive.

Both end with `loop.sh` believing the checkout has no writer while an editing agent holds it. That
breaks the one-writer-per-checkout invariant `docs/parallel_lanes.md` depends on, and it breaks it
precisely when the driver is least observed.

Nothing was corrupted this time, and the margin says why it was luck rather than design: the
concurrent `health:fast` finished at **00:30:00.315** and the orphan's first write landed at
**00:30:17.951** — a **17.6 second** margin. Had the agent woken seventeen seconds earlier, a
green bar would have covered a tree containing unreviewed edits, and the only reason that would
have been caught is that the commit used explicit `git add` paths.

## The fix

`loop.sh` should treat the agent as a process GROUP for its whole lifecycle:

- run the agent command in its own process group, and record that pgid alongside the pid in
  `ai-runs/agent.pid`;
- in the timeout path, signal the GROUP (`kill -TERM -<pgid>`), then poll and escalate to
  `kill -KILL -<pgid>` within the existing kill-after budget;
- before declaring a cycle over — and especially before exiting on the stop file and releasing
  `ai-runs/loop.pid` — verify the group is actually empty, and say so loudly if it is not.

The companion launcher `dev-agent.sh` was hardened separately (agent under `setsid` in its own
group, TERM-then-KILL escalation on trap, verified to end a TERM-ignoring agent in 6s inside the
30s kill-after budget). That covers a stop routed through the launcher. It does NOT cover
`loop.sh`'s own timeout path, which is the automatic one, so the driver half is still open — and a
driver that only kills its own child is only as safe as whatever launcher it happens to be
configured with.

## Acceptance

1. A bash-harness regression in `tests/regression/loop_driver_gates.test.ts` drives the timeout
   path against a stub agent that spawns a TERM-ignoring grandchild, and proves the grandchild is
   dead before the driver reports the cycle result.
2. A second case proves the stop-file path does not remove `ai-runs/loop.pid` while any member of
   the agent's process group is still alive.
3. `ai-runs/agent.pid` records the pgid, so a manual stop can target the group without inferring
   it from `/proc`.
4. No change to the kill-after budget or to any bar.

## Provenance

Observed and contained by the dev-loop manager; pids, timestamps and the 17.6s margin above are
from the live incident, not reconstructed. The lane rule adopted in response — signal the group,
verify via `/proc`, escalate to SIGKILL, never trust a wrapper's exit status — is a workaround for
this defect, not a substitute for it.

evidence.summary: A worker's claude child ignored SIGTERM, outlived the driver by 18m48s, and edited the primary checkout after loop.sh had declared the cycle failed and released the single-writer guard. The driver waits on the agent command, never on its process group.
